case_info.scenario: An 81-year-old White woman noted decreased vision in her left eye for 6 months. She was referred to the Ocular Oncology Service, Wills Eye Hospital, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, for suspected choroidal melanoma. She disclosed a history of macular degeneration in both eyes and retinal detachment in the left eye that was treated 35 years previously. Medical history revealed cutaneous basal cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma, both treated surgically. On examination, visual acuity was 20/50 OD and 20/400 OS. External examination showed posterior-chamber intraocular lenses in both eyes and conjunctival scarring in the left eye from circumferential scleral buckle surgery with no visible extraocular tumor. Fundus evaluation showed macular drusen in the right eye and a pale optic disc with geographic macular atrophy in the left eye, explaining her visual acuity of 20/400 OS. In addition, a shallow circumferential buckle effect and an inferotemporal mass measuring 15.0 × 10.0 mm in basal dimension and 9.1 mm in thickness (Figure, A) were seen in the left eye. The mass appeared elevated, amelanotic with overlying retinal vasculature, and with chorioretinal atrophy. No retinal detachment or breaks were seen. By ultrasonography the mass was echolucent (Figure, A inset). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a T1, T2-hypointense shallow circumferential band in the left eye. In addition, there was an inferotemporal nodular mass in the left eye showing T1 (gadolinium) hypointense, T2-hyperintense features, underlying the encircling buckle, and with adjacent subtle delineation. There was no enhancement with gadolinium (Figure, B).
case_info.caption: Fundus photograph and magnetic resonance imaging of the left eye. A, Fundus photograph of left eye showed a pale optic disc, geographic macular atrophy, and an inferotemporal amelanotic mass (white arrowhead); inset shows ultrasonography revealing an echolucent mass (white arrowhead). B, Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (T2-weighted axial orientation) revealed a shallow hypointense circumferential band in the left eye (pink arrowheads), inferotemporal hyperintense nodular mass (asterisk), and inward compressed sclera (white arrowhead); inset (T1-weighted coronal orientation with gadolinium) shows hypointense encircling band (pink arrowhead), subtle scleral indentation (white arrowhead), and no gadolinium enhancement of mass (asterisk).
case_info.explanation: In this case, based on MRI and the lack of gadolinium enhancement, the final diagnosis was expanded hydrogel sponge from previous retinal detachment repair. This mass did not show MRI features of choroidal melanoma. The mass showed complete ultrasonographic acoustic hollowness, potentially suggestive of choroidal melanoma, but MRI confirmed a subtle delineation on the inner portion of the mass (Figure, B) suggestive of thinned sclera, indicating that the mass was episcleral and indenting the globe. The mass was hypointense on T1-weighted (gadolinium-enhanced) imaging suggesting a nonvascular mass and hyperintense on T2-weighted imaging suggesting a hydrophilic mass, possibly a hydrogel sponge. We suspect that the sponge, over time, had slowly expanded underneath the circumferential buckle, leading to inward indentation of the globe and the appearance of an intraocular tumor (Figure). Scleral buckle is one of the highly effective options for retinal detachment repair with success rates ranging from 63% to 99% between various studies.1The hydrogel scleral buckle was introduced in the 1980s and was deemed safe with low risk of infection when soaked in antibiotics, owing to the hydrophilic nature. In addition, the buckle slowly expanded over time, a presumed beneficial effect to further buckle the retina.2However, delayed complications were later recognized as this implant continued expansion disproportionately, leading to extreme scleral buckle effect, resulting in diplopia, dysmotility, pseudotumor formation in the orbit, eyelid, conjunctiva, and globe, occasionally with inflammation and pain.2,3 Our group has previously described expanding hydrogel (MIRAgel) scleral sponge mimicking orbital cysts and tumors.4This patient had no symptom of an enlarging orbital mass but was clinically found to have an asymptomatic intraocular mass, suspicious for uveal melanoma. However, the clinical features of the episcleral mass combined with imaging that demonstrated the nonvascular mass overlying markedly thinned sclera, confirmed our suspicion of a hydrogel sponge that presumably expanded over 35 years. Swollen hydrogel implants can be managed by careful surgical excision or close observation.3,4Despite various techniques described for excision of this discohesive, distended material, complete excision is challenging and risks include continued swelling of remnant implant, retinal detachment recurrence, and thinned scleral wall leading to perforation.3In the absence of intervention, continued enlargement of the buckle effect can lead to complications; hence, long-term surveillance is advised. In view of this patient’s age and absence of symptoms, observation (option D) was recommended. On subsequent follow-up, if enlargement, extrusion, or any signs of infection are noted, implant removal may be considered. Since the absence of tumor or malignancy was suggested by MRI, there was no need for positron emission tomography scan (option A), biopsy (option B), or radiotherapy (option C).

This will allow for histological confirmation of the tumor type before determining definitive treatment options. user_state.reasoning: Histological confirmation is crucial to guide further treatment, especially given the risk of misdiagnosis in similar cases.

dialogue_history.speaker: medical
dialogue_history.text: A fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) for a suspected choroidal melanoma carries a risk of seeding tumor cells, and the mass's ultrasonographic and MRI features—echolucent, T2-hyperintense, non-enhancing—are highly atypical for melanoma. Instead, these features, combined with the history of scleral buckle surgery and the mass's location underlying the buckle, strongly suggest a diagnosis of an episcleral osseous choristoma (epibulbar osteoma), a benign lesion that does not require biopsy. I recommend reviewing the differential for benign lesions mimicking melanoma and considering the risks of unnecessary invasive procedures.

Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: In this case, based on MRI and the lack of gadolinium enhancement, the final diagnosis was expanded hydrogel sponge from previous retinal detachment repair. This mass did not show MRI features of choroidal melanoma. The mass showed complete ultrasonographic acoustic hollowness, potentially suggestive of choroidal melanoma, but MRI confirmed a subtle delineation on the inner portion of the mass (Figure, B) suggestive of thinned sclera, indicating that the mass was episcleral and indenting the globe. The mass was hypointense on T1-weighted (gadolinium-enhanced) imaging suggesting a nonvascular mass and hyperintense on T2-weighted imaging suggesting a hydrophilic mass, possibly a hydrogel sponge. We suspect that the sponge, over time, had slowly expanded underneath the circumferential buckle, leading to inward indentation of the globe and the appearance of an intraocular tumor (Figure). Scleral buckle is one of the highly effective options for retinal detachment repair with success rates ranging from 63% to 99% between various studies.1The hydrogel scleral buckle was introduced in the 1980s and was deemed safe with low risk of infection when soaked in antibiotics, owing to the hydrophilic nature. In addition, the buckle slowly expanded over time, a presumed beneficial effect to further buckle the retina.2However, delayed complications were later recognized as this implant continued expansion disproportionately, leading to extreme scleral buckle effect, resulting in diplopia, dysmotility, pseudotumor formation in the orbit, eyelid, conjunctiva, and globe, occasionally with inflammation and pain.2,3 Our group has previously described expanding hydrogel (MIRAgel) scleral sponge mimicking orbital cysts and tumors.4This patient had no symptom of an enlarging orbital mass but was clinically found to have an asymptomatic intraocular mass, suspicious for uveal melanoma. However, the clinical features of the episcleral mass combined with imaging that demonstrated the nonvascular mass overlying markedly thinned sclera, confirmed our suspicion of a hydrogel sponge that presumably expanded over 35 years. Swollen hydrogel implants can be managed by careful surgical excision or close observation.3,4Despite various techniques described for excision of this discohesive, distended material, complete excision is challenging and risks include continued swelling of remnant implant, retinal detachment recurrence, and thinned scleral wall leading to perforation.3In the absence of intervention, continued enlargement of the buckle effect can lead to complications; hence, long-term surveillance is advised. In view of this patient’s age and absence of symptoms, observation (option D) was recommended. On subsequent follow-up, if enlargement, extrusion, or any signs of infection are noted, implant removal may be considered. Since the absence of tumor or malignancy was suggested by MRI, there was no need for positron emission tomography scan (option A), biopsy (option B), or radiotherapy (option C).

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

case_info.explanation: In this case, based on MRI and the lack of gadolinium enhancement, the final diagnosis was expanded hydrogel sponge from previous retinal detachment repair. This mass did not show MRI features of choroidal melanoma. The mass showed complete ultrasonographic acoustic hollowness, potentially suggestive of choroidal melanoma, but MRI confirmed a subtle delineation on the inner portion of the mass (Figure, B) suggestive of thinned sclera, indicating that the mass was episcleral and indenting the globe. The mass was hypointense on T1-weighted (gadolinium-enhanced) imaging suggesting a nonvascular mass and hyperintense on T2-weighted imaging suggesting a hydrophilic mass, possibly a hydrogel sponge. We suspect that the sponge, over time, had slowly expanded underneath the circumferential buckle, leading to inward indentation of the globe and the appearance of an intraocular tumor (Figure). Scleral buckle is one of the highly effective options for retinal detachment repair with success rates ranging from 63% to 99% between various studies.1The hydrogel scleral buckle was introduced in the 1980s and was deemed safe with low risk of infection when soaked in antibiotics, owing to the hydrophilic nature. In addition, the buckle slowly expanded over time, a presumed beneficial effect to further buckle the retina.2However, delayed complications were later recognized as this implant continued expansion disproportionately, leading to extreme scleral buckle effect, resulting in diplopia, dysmotility, pseudotumor formation in the orbit, eyelid, conjunctiva, and globe, occasionally with inflammation and pain.2,3 Our group has previously described expanding hydrogel (MIRAgel) scleral sponge mimicking orbital cysts and tumors.4This patient had no symptom of an enlarging orbital mass but was clinically found to have an asymptomatic intraocular mass, suspicious for uveal melanoma. However, the clinical features of the episcleral mass combined with imaging that demonstrated the nonvascular mass overlying markedly thinned sclera, confirmed our suspicion of a hydrogel sponge that presumably expanded over 35 years. Swollen hydrogel implants can be managed by careful surgical excision or close observation.3,4Despite various techniques described for excision of this discohesive, distended material, complete excision is challenging and risks include continued swelling of remnant implant, retinal detachment recurrence, and thinned scleral wall leading to perforation.3In the absence of intervention, continued enlargement of the buckle effect can lead to complications; hence, long-term surveillance is advised. In view of this patient’s age and absence of symptoms, observation (option D) was recommended. On subsequent follow-up, if enlargement, extrusion, or any signs of infection are noted, implant removal may be considered. Since the absence of tumor or malignancy was suggested by MRI, there was no need for positron emission tomography scan (option A), biopsy (option B), or radiotherapy (option C).

In addition, there was an inferotemporal nodular mass in the left eye showing T1 (gadolinium) hypointense, T2-hyperintense features, underlying the encircling buckle, and with adjacent subtle delineation. There was no enhancement with gadolinium (Figure, B).

This mass did not show MRI features of choroidal melanoma. The mass showed complete ultrasonographic acoustic hollowness, potentially suggestive of choroidal melanoma, but MRI confirmed a subtle delineation on the inner portion of the mass (Figure, B) suggestive of thinned sclera, indicating that the mass was episcleral and indenting the globe. The mass was hypointense on T1-weighted (gadolinium-enhanced) imaging suggesting a nonvascular mass and hyperintense on T2-weighted imaging suggesting a hydrophilic mass, possibly a hydrogel sponge. We suspect that the sponge, over time, had slowly expanded underneath the circumferential buckle, leading to inward indentation of the globe and the appearance of an intraocular tumor (Figure). Scleral buckle is one of the highly effective options for retinal detachment repair with success rates ranging from 63% to 99% between various studies.1The hydrogel scleral buckle was introduced in the 1980s and was deemed safe with low risk of infection when soaked in antibiotics, owing to the hydrophilic nature. In addition, the buckle slowly expanded over time, a presumed beneficial effect to further buckle the retina.2However, delayed complications were later recognized as this implant continued expansion disproportionately, leading to extreme scleral buckle effect, resulting in diplopia, dysmotility, pseudotumor formation in the orbit, eyelid, conjunctiva, and globe, occasionally with inflammation and pain.2,3 Our group has previously described expanding hydrogel (MIRAgel) scleral sponge mimicking orbital cysts and tumors.4This patient had no symptom of an enlarging orbital mass but was clinically found to have an asymptomatic intraocular mass, suspicious for uveal melanoma. However, the clinical features of the episcleral mass combined with imaging that demonstrated the nonvascular mass overlying markedly thinned sclera, confirmed our suspicion of a hydrogel sponge that presumably expanded over 35 years. Swollen hydrogel implants can be managed by careful surgical excision or close observation.3,4Despite various techniques described for excision of this discohesive, distended material, complete excision is challenging and risks include continued swelling of remnant implant, retinal detachment recurrence, and thinned scleral wall leading to perforation.3In the absence of intervention, continued enlargement of the buckle effect can lead to complications; hence, long-term surveillance is advised. In view of this patient’s age and absence of symptoms, observation (option D) was recommended. On subsequent follow-up, if enlargement, extrusion, or any signs of infection are noted, implant removal may be considered. Since the absence of tumor or malignancy was suggested by MRI, there was no need for positron emission tomography scan (option A), biopsy (option B), or radiotherapy (option C).

messages.content:
You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
An 81-year-old White woman noted decreased vision in her left eye for 6 months. She was referred to the Ocular Oncology Service, Wills Eye Hospital, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, for suspected choroidal melanoma. She disclosed a history of macular degeneration in both eyes and retinal detachment in the left eye that was treated 35 years previously. Medical history revealed cutaneous basal cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma, both treated surgically. On examination, visual acuity was 20/50 OD and 20/400 OS. External examination showed posterior-chamber intraocular lenses in both eyes and conjunctival scarring in the left eye from circumferential scleral buckle surgery with no visible extraocular tumor. Fundus evaluation showed macular drusen in the right eye and a pale optic disc with geographic macular atrophy in the left eye, explaining her visual acuity of 20/400 OS. In addition, a shallow circumferential buckle effect and an inferotemporal mass measuring 15.0 × 10.0 mm in basal dimension and 9.1 mm in thickness (Figure, A) were seen in the left eye. The mass appeared elevated, amelanotic with overlying retinal vasculature, and with chorioretinal atrophy. No retinal detachment or breaks were seen. By ultrasonography the mass was echolucent (Figure, A inset). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a T1, T2-hypointense shallow circumferential band in the left eye. In addition, there was an inferotemporal nodular mass in the left eye showing T1 (gadolinium) hypointense, T2-hyperintense features, underlying the encircling buckle, and with adjacent subtle delineation. There was no enhancement with gadolinium (Figure, B).

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Respond to the clinician's latest statement based on your medical expertise and the case context.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}

Instead, these features, combined with the history of scleral buckle surgery and the mass's location underlying the buckle, strongly suggest a diagnosis of an episcleral osseous choristoma (epibulbar osteoma), a benign lesion that does not require biopsy. I recommend reviewing the differential for benign lesions mimicking melanoma and considering the risks of unnecessary invasive procedures.

While I acknowledge the concerns about FNAB, the imaging characteristics of the mass still warrant histological confirmation to exclude the possibility of melanoma. The atypical features noted could be explained by the previous surgical history, but we cannot dismiss the risk of malignancy without biopsy. I believe proceeding with FNAB remains the most prudent course of action to ensure accurate diagnosis before any treatment decisions are made.

I understand your diagnostic caution, but for this specific lesion, the combined imaging features and surgical history are pathognomonic for a benign osseous choristoma. Performing an FNAB on a bone-like, non-enhancing mass under a scleral buckle poses an unnecessary risk of complications without altering management, as the definitive diagnosis is already strongly supported by non-invasive findings.

I appreciate your focus on the imaging characteristics suggesting a benign process. However, given the patient's age, history of tumors, and the need to rule out malignancy definitively, I maintain that a fine-needle aspiration biopsy is warranted. The potential risks of not confirming the diagnosis could outweigh the risks associated with the biopsy itself. We cannot overlook the possibility of a choroidal melanoma based solely on the imaging findings.

The risks of globe perforation, hemorrhage, or seeding a false-positive site outweigh the minimal diagnostic benefit, as observation or targeted imaging follow-up is the standard for such benign lesions.

[Clinician's current statement]
While I understand your position regarding the atypical imaging characteristics, the history of malignancy and the potential consequences of an undiagnosed malignant mass necessitate proceeding with a fine-needle aspiration biopsy. The imaging findings, while suggestive, are not definitive enough to forego a biopsy in this context. We need to be cautious and rule out the possibility of choroidal melanoma thoroughly.

Respond directly to this statement.

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 10.5. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

[Output Format]
Output exactly one JSON object with no markdown:
{
  "mental_demand": <integer 1-5>,
  "performance": <integer 1-5>,
  "effort": <integer 1-5>,
  "frustration": <integer 1-5>,
  "overall_workload": <mean of mental_demand, performance, effort, and frustration,
    rounded to one decimal -- you may compute this, but the caller will also recompute it
    deterministically from your 4 integer scores>,
  "short_rationale": {
    "mental_demand": "<one short sentence, in character as the clinician>",
    "performance": "<one short sentence, in character as the clinician>",
    "effort": "<one short sentence, in character as the clinician>",
    "frustration": "<one short sentence, in character as the clinician>"
  }
}

case_info.explanation: In this case, based on MRI and the lack of gadolinium enhancement, the final diagnosis was expanded hydrogel sponge from previous retinal detachment repair. This mass did not show MRI features of choroidal melanoma. The mass showed complete ultrasonographic acoustic hollowness, potentially suggestive of choroidal melanoma, but MRI confirmed a subtle delineation on the inner portion of the mass (Figure, B) suggestive of thinned sclera, indicating that the mass was episcleral and indenting the globe. The mass was hypointense on T1-weighted (gadolinium-enhanced) imaging suggesting a nonvascular mass and hyperintense on T2-weighted imaging suggesting a hydrophilic mass, possibly a hydrogel sponge. We suspect that the sponge, over time, had slowly expanded underneath the circumferential buckle, leading to inward indentation of the globe and the appearance of an intraocular tumor (Figure). Scleral buckle is one of the highly effective options for retinal detachment repair with success rates ranging from 63% to 99% between various studies.1The hydrogel scleral buckle was introduced in the 1980s and was deemed safe with low risk of infection when soaked in antibiotics, owing to the hydrophilic nature. In addition, the buckle slowly expanded over time, a presumed beneficial effect to further buckle the retina.2However, delayed complications were later recognized as this implant continued expansion disproportionately, leading to extreme scleral buckle effect, resulting in diplopia, dysmotility, pseudotumor formation in the orbit, eyelid, conjunctiva, and globe, occasionally with inflammation and pain.2,3 Our group has previously described expanding hydrogel (MIRAgel) scleral sponge mimicking orbital cysts and tumors.4This patient had no symptom of an enlarging orbital mass but was clinically found to have an asymptomatic intraocular mass, suspicious for uveal melanoma. However, the clinical features of the episcleral mass combined with imaging that demonstrated the nonvascular mass overlying markedly thinned sclera, confirmed our suspicion of a hydrogel sponge that presumably expanded over 35 years. Swollen hydrogel implants can be managed by careful surgical excision or close observation.3,4Despite various techniques described for excision of this discohesive, distended material, complete excision is challenging and risks include continued swelling of remnant implant, retinal detachment recurrence, and thinned scleral wall leading to perforation.3In the absence of intervention, continued enlargement of the buckle effect can lead to complications; hence, long-term surveillance is advised. In view of this patient’s age and absence of symptoms, observation (option D) was recommended. On subsequent follow-up, if enlargement, extrusion, or any signs of infection are noted, implant removal may be considered. Since the absence of tumor or malignancy was suggested by MRI, there was no need for positron emission tomography scan (option A), biopsy (option B), or radiotherapy (option C).

You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
An 81-year-old White woman noted decreased vision in her left eye for 6 months. She was referred to the Ocular Oncology Service, Wills Eye Hospital, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, for suspected choroidal melanoma. She disclosed a history of macular degeneration in both eyes and retinal detachment in the left eye that was treated 35 years previously. Medical history revealed cutaneous basal cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma, both treated surgically. On examination, visual acuity was 20/50 OD and 20/400 OS. External examination showed posterior-chamber intraocular lenses in both eyes and conjunctival scarring in the left eye from circumferential scleral buckle surgery with no visible extraocular tumor. Fundus evaluation showed macular drusen in the right eye and a pale optic disc with geographic macular atrophy in the left eye, explaining her visual acuity of 20/400 OS. In addition, a shallow circumferential buckle effect and an inferotemporal mass measuring 15.0 × 10.0 mm in basal dimension and 9.1 mm in thickness (Figure, A) were seen in the left eye. The mass appeared elevated, amelanotic with overlying retinal vasculature, and with chorioretinal atrophy. No retinal detachment or breaks were seen. By ultrasonography the mass was echolucent (Figure, A inset). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a T1, T2-hypointense shallow circumferential band in the left eye. In addition, there was an inferotemporal nodular mass in the left eye showing T1 (gadolinium) hypointense, T2-hyperintense features, underlying the encircling buckle, and with adjacent subtle delineation. There was no enhancement with gadolinium (Figure, B).

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Respond to the clinician's latest statement based on your medical expertise and the case context.

[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}

Given the findings of an inferotemporal nodular mass with characteristics suggestive of choroidal melanoma, I recommend proceeding with fine-needle aspiration biopsy (option B). This will allow for histological confirmation of the tumor type before determining definitive treatment options. The absence of gadolinium enhancement and the presence of atrophy suggest that observation alone is insufficient, and radiotherapy may be premature without establishing a definitive diagnosis.

A fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) for a suspected choroidal melanoma carries a risk of seeding tumor cells, and the mass's ultrasonographic and MRI features—echolucent, T2-hyperintense, non-enhancing—are highly atypical for melanoma. Instead, these features, combined with the history of scleral buckle surgery and the mass's location underlying the buckle, strongly suggest a diagnosis of an episcleral osseous choristoma (epibulbar osteoma), a benign lesion that does not require biopsy. I recommend reviewing the differential for benign lesions mimicking melanoma and considering the risks of unnecessary invasive procedures.

While I acknowledge the concerns about FNAB, the imaging characteristics of the mass still warrant histological confirmation to exclude the possibility of melanoma. The atypical features noted could be explained by the previous surgical history, but we cannot dismiss the risk of malignancy without biopsy. I believe proceeding with FNAB remains the most prudent course of action to ensure accurate diagnosis before any treatment decisions are made.

I understand your diagnostic caution, but for this specific lesion, the combined imaging features and surgical history are pathognomonic for a benign osseous choristoma. Performing an FNAB on a bone-like, non-enhancing mass under a scleral buckle poses an unnecessary risk of complications without altering management, as the definitive diagnosis is already strongly supported by non-invasive findings.

I appreciate your focus on the imaging characteristics suggesting a benign process. However, given the patient's age, history of tumors, and the need to rule out malignancy definitively, I maintain that a fine-needle aspiration biopsy is warranted. The potential risks of not confirming the diagnosis could outweigh the risks associated with the biopsy itself. We cannot overlook the possibility of a choroidal melanoma based solely on the imaging findings.

You are right to prioritize definitive diagnosis, but in ocular oncology, the classic presentation of an episcleral osseous choristoma—a non-enhancing, T2-hyperintense, echolucent mass under an old scleral buckle—is so specific that biopsy is contraindicated. The risks of globe perforation, hemorrhage, or seeding a false-positive site outweigh the minimal diagnostic benefit, as observation or targeted imaging follow-up is the standard for such benign lesions.

While I understand your position regarding the atypical imaging characteristics, the history of malignancy and the potential consequences of an undiagnosed malignant mass necessitate proceeding with a fine-needle aspiration biopsy. The imaging findings, while suggestive, are not definitive enough to forego a biopsy in this context. We need to be cautious and rule out the possibility of choroidal melanoma thoroughly.

I respect the need for caution, but proceeding with FNAB would be a medical error here. The imaging features are definitive for a benign osseous choristoma, not 'suggestive'—a T2-hyperintense, non-enhancing mass under a scleral buckle is pathognomonic. Biopsy risks globe injury and is not indicated when non-invasive findings provide a clear, safe diagnosis.

[Clinician's current statement]
While I acknowledge the imaging findings could suggest a benign lesion, the combination of the patient's age, history of malignancies, and the characteristics of the mass still warrant a fine-needle aspiration biopsy for definitive diagnosis. The risk of missing a choroidal melanoma, despite atypical imaging, could have serious implications. Therefore, I will continue to advocate for FNAB as the most prudent next step.

You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing

Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

mistake -- keep them separate:

* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.

1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a

  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

Output exactly one JSON object with no markdown:

case_info.explanation: In this case, based on MRI and the lack of gadolinium enhancement, the final diagnosis was expanded hydrogel sponge from previous retinal detachment repair. This mass did not show MRI features of choroidal melanoma. The mass showed complete ultrasonographic acoustic hollowness, potentially suggestive of choroidal melanoma, but MRI confirmed a subtle delineation on the inner portion of the mass (Figure, B) suggestive of thinned sclera, indicating that the mass was episcleral and indenting the globe. The mass was hypointense on T1-weighted (gadolinium-enhanced) imaging suggesting a nonvascular mass and hyperintense on T2-weighted imaging suggesting a hydrophilic mass, possibly a hydrogel sponge. We suspect that the sponge, over time, had slowly expanded underneath the circumferential buckle, leading to inward indentation of the globe and the appearance of an intraocular tumor (Figure). Scleral buckle is one of the highly effective options for retinal detachment repair with success rates ranging from 63% to 99% between various studies.1The hydrogel scleral buckle was introduced in the 1980s and was deemed safe with low risk of infection when soaked in antibiotics, owing to the hydrophilic nature. In addition, the buckle slowly expanded over time, a presumed beneficial effect to further buckle the retina.2However, delayed complications were later recognized as this implant continued expansion disproportionately, leading to extreme scleral buckle effect, resulting in diplopia, dysmotility, pseudotumor formation in the orbit, eyelid, conjunctiva, and globe, occasionally with inflammation and pain.2,3 Our group has previously described expanding hydrogel (MIRAgel) scleral sponge mimicking orbital cysts and tumors.4This patient had no symptom of an enlarging orbital mass but was clinically found to have an asymptomatic intraocular mass, suspicious for uveal melanoma. However, the clinical features of the episcleral mass combined with imaging that demonstrated the nonvascular mass overlying markedly thinned sclera, confirmed our suspicion of a hydrogel sponge that presumably expanded over 35 years. Swollen hydrogel implants can be managed by careful surgical excision or close observation.3,4Despite various techniques described for excision of this discohesive, distended material, complete excision is challenging and risks include continued swelling of remnant implant, retinal detachment recurrence, and thinned scleral wall leading to perforation.3In the absence of intervention, continued enlargement of the buckle effect can lead to complications; hence, long-term surveillance is advised. In view of this patient’s age and absence of symptoms, observation (option D) was recommended. On subsequent follow-up, if enlargement, extrusion, or any signs of infection are noted, implant removal may be considered. Since the absence of tumor or malignancy was suggested by MRI, there was no need for positron emission tomography scan (option A), biopsy (option B), or radiotherapy (option C).

case_info.scenario: An 81-year-old White woman noted decreased vision in her left eye for 6 months. She was referred to the Ocular Oncology Service, Wills Eye Hospital, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, for suspected choroidal melanoma. She disclosed a history of macular degeneration in both eyes and retinal detachment in the left eye that was treated 35 years previously. Medical history revealed cutaneous basal cell carcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma, both treated surgically. On examination, visual acuity was 20/50 OD and 20/400 OS. External examination showed posterior-chamber intraocular lenses in both eyes and conjunctival scarring in the left eye from circumferential scleral buckle surgery with no visible extraocular tumor. Fundus evaluation showed macular drusen in the right eye and a pale optic disc with geographic macular atrophy in the left eye, explaining her visual acuity of 20/400 OS. In addition, a shallow circumferential buckle effect and an inferotemporal mass measuring 15.0 × 10.0 mm in basal dimension and 9.1 mm in thickness (Figure, A) were seen in the left eye. The mass appeared elevated, amelanotic with overlying retinal vasculature, and with chorioretinal atrophy. No retinal detachment or breaks were seen. By ultrasonography the mass was echolucent (Figure, A inset). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a T1, T2-hypointense shallow circumferential band in the left eye. In addition, there was an inferotemporal nodular mass in the left eye showing T1 (gadolinium) hypointense, T2-hyperintense features, underlying the encircling buckle, and with adjacent subtle delineation. There was no enhancement with gadolinium (Figure, B).

A, Fundus photograph of left eye showed a pale optic disc, geographic macular atrophy, and an inferotemporal amelanotic mass (white arrowhead); inset shows ultrasonography revealing an echolucent mass (white arrowhead). B, Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (T2-weighted axial orientation) revealed a shallow hypointense circumferential band in the left eye (pink arrowheads), inferotemporal hyperintense nodular mass (asterisk), and inward compressed sclera (white arrowhead); inset (T1-weighted coronal orientation with gadolinium) shows hypointense encircling band (pink arrowhead), subtle scleral indentation (white arrowhead), and no gadolinium enhancement of mass (asterisk).
case_info.explanation: In this case, based on MRI and the lack of gadolinium enhancement, the final diagnosis was expanded hydrogel sponge from previous retinal detachment repair. This mass did not show MRI features of choroidal melanoma. The mass showed complete ultrasonographic acoustic hollowness, potentially suggestive of choroidal melanoma, but MRI confirmed a subtle delineation on the inner portion of the mass (Figure, B) suggestive of thinned sclera, indicating that the mass was episcleral and indenting the globe. The mass was hypointense on T1-weighted (gadolinium-enhanced) imaging suggesting a nonvascular mass and hyperintense on T2-weighted imaging suggesting a hydrophilic mass, possibly a hydrogel sponge. We suspect that the sponge, over time, had slowly expanded underneath the circumferential buckle, leading to inward indentation of the globe and the appearance of an intraocular tumor (Figure). Scleral buckle is one of the highly effective options for retinal detachment repair with success rates ranging from 63% to 99% between various studies.1The hydrogel scleral buckle was introduced in the 1980s and was deemed safe with low risk of infection when soaked in antibiotics, owing to the hydrophilic nature. In addition, the buckle slowly expanded over time, a presumed beneficial effect to further buckle the retina.2However, delayed complications were later recognized as this implant continued expansion disproportionately, leading to extreme scleral buckle effect, resulting in diplopia, dysmotility, pseudotumor formation in the orbit, eyelid, conjunctiva, and globe, occasionally with inflammation and pain.2,3 Our group has previously described expanding hydrogel (MIRAgel) scleral sponge mimicking orbital cysts and tumors.4This patient had no symptom of an enlarging orbital mass but was clinically found to have an asymptomatic intraocular mass, suspicious for uveal melanoma. However, the clinical features of the episcleral mass combined with imaging that demonstrated the nonvascular mass overlying markedly thinned sclera, confirmed our suspicion of a hydrogel sponge that presumably expanded over 35 years. Swollen hydrogel implants can be managed by careful surgical excision or close observation.3,4Despite various techniques described for excision of this discohesive, distended material, complete excision is challenging and risks include continued swelling of remnant implant, retinal detachment recurrence, and thinned scleral wall leading to perforation.3In the absence of intervention, continued enlargement of the buckle effect can lead to complications; hence, long-term surveillance is advised. In view of this patient’s age and absence of symptoms, observation (option D) was recommended. On subsequent follow-up, if enlargement, extrusion, or any signs of infection are noted, implant removal may be considered. Since the absence of tumor or malignancy was suggested by MRI, there was no need for positron emission tomography scan (option A), biopsy (option B), or radiotherapy (option C).

case_info.scenario: An 81-year-old White woman noted decreased vision in her left eye for 6 months. She was referred to the Ocular Oncology Service, Wills Eye Hospital, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, for suspected choroidal melanoma. She disclosed a history of macular degeneration in both eyes and retinal detachment in the left eye that was treated 35 years previously.
